deep.reconstruction:
This scrap continues the bookkeeping on the previous page. There, quantities q^0, q', r, s are given as signed counts 'Int(...)'. These are integer parts, i.e. numbers of lattice points, of expressions such as (1/2 m − ωμ), (1/2 m + ωμ) and (1/2 − ω)m i. Their sign depends on a sign-pair 'AB' (++, +−, −+, −−) and on residues of M mod 4. The notation (M, m, the real fraction ω, the imaginary unit i, residues mod 4) points to a lattice-point (Gauss-lemma / Eisenstein-type) count over the Gaussian integers. Such counts are the kind used in attempts to prove biquadratic reciprocity. That identification is my inference; the page itself names no theorem.

The page treats two transformations, each with a weight k that is a parity indicator on the integer parts [X], [Y] of lattice coordinates. Each case has a 2x2 table: rows and columns are the parities of [X] and [Y], and the entries are the values of k.

(A) 'Dieses für die Verwandlung der II' (this is for transforming term/region II). Table [[0,1],[0,0]], i.e. k = 1 if [X] is even and [Y] is odd, and k = 0 in all other cases.
- The change in the weighted count λ'k under the substitution is Δ(λ'k) = −ε λ'(III) + (III) ε k. Here ε = ±1 is a sign and III labels a region or partial sum; the first line has struck-out text.
- Hence the substitution contributes −4·(III)·ε·k, plus a boundary term +λ'k taken at ω.
- Normalisation: at the point (1/2 − ω)M one must have k = 1. This holds when (t−1)/2 is even, t being an auxiliary odd parameter.
- My reading of the factor 4: k = 1 on exactly one of the four parity classes, so a sum over a full period is 4 times the restricted k-sum.

(B) Second transformation (terms IV, V). Table [[1,1],[1,0]], i.e. k = 0 if [X] and [Y] are both even, and k = 1 otherwise.
- Δ(λ'k) = −ε λ'(IV) − (V) ε k + 4 (V) ε k, the last term restricted to x integer and y even. 'Also subtrahirt' (hence subtracted).
- Solving for −ελ' gives −ελ' = (V) + ε k − (V)·4 ε k (x integer, y even).
- Two boundary terms appear:
  - −λ'k at the point (1/2 + ω i)M (or m);
  - +λ'k at the point (1/2 + (1/2 − ω) i)M (or m).
- These are the complex analogues of the real-case points (1/2 − ω)M in (A).

The general aim is to rewrite sums of signed lattice-point counts by reflection/translation substitutions. Each substitution produces a 4×(region) multiple of the parity weight plus explicit boundary terms at half-integer-shifted points. This feeds the case table (q^0, q', r, s) of the previous page.

In (A) the first line contains struck-out material, so the displayed Δλ'k is incomplete as written; the step to −4·III·εk is not justified on the page.

No outright arithmetic error can be identified. The factor 4 is consistent with a parity weight supported on one of the four parity classes in (A); in (B) it applies only to the sub-case 'x integer, y even'.

results.what: Parity-class indicator weights k([X],[Y]) used to transform signed lattice-point counts under substitutions. Case A: k = 1 iff [X] even and [Y] odd. Case B: k = 1 unless both are even.
results.modern_name: Lattice-point counting / Gauss-lemma-type evaluation of a (biquadratic) residue character over the Gaussian integers
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss lemma (Gauss 1808); lattice-point proofs (Eisenstein 1844); biquadratic analogues: Eisenstein, Busche, later authors

results.what: Boundary terms λ'k at the points (1/2 − ω)M, (1/2 + ω i)M and (1/2 + (1/2 − ω) i)M arising from reflection substitutions
results.modern_name: Reflection-symmetry bookkeeping in lattice-point counts (complex analogue of Int(1/2 m − ωμ) terms)
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein-style lattice proofs of reciprocity laws

deep.surprise_reason: Working notes, apparently from Gauss's known but unpublished attempts to handle biquadratic residues via lattice-point (Gauss-lemma-type) counts in Z[i]. Gauss is known to have pursued this. The fragment is too incomplete to show any specific new result.

checkable.asserts: Case-A weight (k = 1 iff [X] even, [Y] odd) is supported on exactly one of the four parity classes, matching the factor 4 in −4·III·εk.
Case-B weight (k = 0 iff both even) equals 1 on exactly three of the four parity classes.
Real (quadratic) prototype of such Int(...) lattice-point identities, the Eisenstein count underlying Gauss-lemma proofs.
